notes.b: Choosing child care starts with the family, not the service. A family's working pattern, support network, budget and school calendar decide which options are even possible.
points: Working pattern: whether both parents, or a lone parent, are in paid work, and how many hours each works. Shift work or irregular hours need a more flexible carer than a regular nine-to-five job.
Support network: whether grandparents, other relatives or friends are available and willing to mind the child. If they are, the family may need little or no paid care.
Cost: what the family can afford to pay, which may limit the options available. Some families qualify for a State subsidy towards the cost of registered child care.
After-school and holiday cover: school closing times and school holidays create gaps that the family must fill, because school usually finishes before work does and the holidays are long.
notes.tip: If asked to summarise the factors that influence a family's child care needs, give a short phrase for each one: working pattern, relatives, cost, after-school and holiday cover, availability, hours, proximity, the child's age or needs, reliability and quality.

notes.h: Family requirements: the service and the child
notes.b: Once the family's situation is clear, it must be matched to what a service can actually offer. These requirements test whether an option is practical, reliable and right for the child.
points: Availability and convenience: the option must have a place free and be open at the times needed, and be reachable without a long journey.
Hours and flexibility: the option must cover the parents' hours, including early starts, late finishes and changing shifts.
Proximity: a service near home, school or work reduces travel time for the child and the parent.
Child's age or special needs: the option must suit the child's stage of development and any additional care needs, including health needs.
Reliability: the option must stay open during staff illness and closures, so that the parent is not left without cover if the carer is ill or the service closes.
Quality: safety and hygiene, staff qualifications, the activities provided and the ratio of staff to children all matter, as do the parents' trust in the carer and whether the child is happy there.
notes.tip: Examiners accept this list as a summary answer, so give each requirement as a short phrase tied to a family's situation rather than writing a long paragraph on one.

notes.h: Types of child care: full-day and home-based care
notes.b: Some options care for children for the whole working day. They differ in who the carer is, where the care happens and who employs them.
points: Crèche or day nursery: a centre with trained staff that cares for children in groups during the working day, usually open all day, in premises used for that purpose, with structured routines and play.

Childminder: an adult who minds one or a small number of children in the minder's own home. The setting is a home, the attention is personal and the hours are often flexible. A childminder is self-employed.
Nanny: a carer employed by the family, who usually looks after the children of that one family in the family home. The family is the employer.

Au pair: a young person, often from abroad, who lives with the host family and provides childcare and does light household duties in exchange for board and pocket money. An au pair is not a trained carer or nanny, works limited hours and suits older children or extra support.

Relative or friend: a grandparent, aunt, uncle or friend who minds the child informally. This is usually low cost or free and familiar and trusted, but it depends on the helper's health and availability.
Employer or workplace crèche: care provided at or near the workplace by the employer, which saves the parent a separate journey.
notes.tip: Do not blur the roles. A nanny is employed by the family in the family's home, a childminder is self-employed in the minder's own home, and an au pair is not a trained nanny or an ordinary employee.

notes.h: Types of child care: after-school and pre-school options
notes.b: Other options fill part of the day. After-school groups cover the gap when school ends, while pre-school services give younger children a few hours of play and learning.
points: After-school group: a service that collects children from school and cares for them until a parent finishes work. Some also run holiday or summer camps and may offer homework help and activities.
Playschool or playgroup: a sessional service (one that runs in set sessions) for pre-school children, mainly play-based, usually for a few hours in the morning or afternoon.
Montessori: a pre-school method, following the educational ideas of Maria Montessori, that encourages self-directed learning through structured materials and activities.
Naíonra: an Irish-medium pre-school (naíonraí is the plural), where the children learn through the Irish language by play. Naíonraí are supported by Forbairt Naíonraí.

Pre-school under the national free pre-school scheme (ECCE): State-funded pre-school hours in the year or years before primary school, in registered services, so the family does not pay for the funded sessions.
notes.tip: Pre-school is not only for working parents. Playschools, Montessori schools and naíonraí are also educational, so say so when asked to describe them.

notes.h: Regulation and quality of child care
notes.b: Parents hand their children to carers they do not supervise, so the State regulates child care. Knowing who registers and inspects a service tells parents what to check before they choose.
points: Early years services (crèches, playschools, Montessori schools, naíonraí and after-school services) must be registered with Tusla, the Child and Family Agency. Tusla's early years inspectorate inspects them under the Child Care Act 1991 (Early Years Services) Regulations 2016.
This is why parents should check that a service is registered and read its inspection reports. Staff-to-child ratios are set by regulation.

Childminders: the Child Care (Amendment) Act 2024 and the Child Care Act 1991 (Early Years Services) (Childminding Services) Regulations 2024 bring childminders into Tusla registration. Registration opened on 30 September 2024 and is currently voluntary, with mandatory registration due after a transition period.

Registered childminders can take part in the National Childcare Scheme. Parents should ask whether a childminder is registered, has training, Garda vetting (a police check), references, insurance and emergency cover.
The National Childcare Scheme (NCS) is the State's scheme that subsidises the cost of registered child care according to the family's circumstances.

notes.h: Benefits of pre-school education for children
notes.b: Pre-school is more than minding children while parents work. It is the first place many children learn to mix with others and begin to learn, which prepares them for primary school.
points: Children become more socially aware by playing and interacting with other children.
Children form relationships outside the home and learn to share and take turns.
Children become more independent and confident when they are cared for away from their parents.
Intellectual development is supported through activities that build language, number, listening, problem-solving and creativity skills, which also prepares children for primary school.
Physical development is supported through games and active play, which build coordination and fine motor skills (the small, precise movements of hands and fingers).
Emotional development: children learn to separate from their parents, which builds self-esteem.
Pre-school also helps working parents, because the child is cared for in a safe, structured setting.
notes.tip: For the benefits of pre-school, cover social, intellectual and physical development, plus independence and confidence, and give a reason or example for each.

notes.b: A crèche suits parents with regular hours who want trained staff and structure. Its strengths come from being a larger, organised centre, and its weaknesses come from the same thing.
points: Advantages: fixed daily opening hours, which suit parents with regular working patterns and make the service reliable.
Advantages: several staff care for a group of children, so cover is available when one staff member is absent.
Advantages: structured activities and peer play (play with other children) support the child's social and intellectual development.
Advantages: staff often hold early-childhood qualifications and work to a written programme, and the service is registered and inspected.
Disadvantages: fixed hours give little flexibility when a parent's shift changes at short notice, and travel must happen at set times.
Disadvantages: group care exposes young children to infections, so they may be ill more often.
Disadvantages: fees are often charged by the session or by the week, and can be a significant cost for the family.
Disadvantages: the child gets less individual attention and may be unsettled by a large group.
notes.tip: Always give both strengths and weaknesses of an option and say which family it suits, for example parents with regular hours who want trained staff.

notes.b: A childminder offers a small, home-like setting, which many parents prefer for babies and young children. The trade-off is that everything depends on one person.
points: Advantages: care is given in a home setting with a small group, which suits very young children and babies.
Advantages: childminders are often able to offer flexible or extended hours.
Advantages: the child receives individual attention and the minder may collect children from school.
Advantages: a childminder is often cheaper for a family with several children.
Disadvantages: the service depends on one adult, so illness, holidays or an emergency can leave the family without cover.
Disadvantages: the range of planned educational activities may be narrower than in a larger centre, and there are fewer facilities.
Disadvantages: quality depends on the minder, so the family must check registration with Tusla, experience, training, vetting, safety and insurance before making a decision.
notes.tip: Do not say parents need only check insurance. Registration with Tusla is now part of what a parent should check, along with experience, training, safety and insurance.

notes.h: Criteria for evaluating a child care option
notes.b: To judge any option fairly, a family uses the same set of criteria each time. These criteria come straight from the family's requirements.
points: Cost: the total weekly cost, including fees, extras such as meals or outings, and the cost of travel.
Hours and location: whether the opening hours and the journey time fit the parents' working day.
Hygiene and safety: cleanliness of premises, safe equipment, secure entry and a safety policy.
Staff qualifications and training: the level of early-childhood training held by the staff, and the ratio of staff to children.
Staffing cover: what happens when a staff member is ill or on leave.
Activities and learning: the play, learning and outdoor activities provided for the child's age.
Suitability for the child: whether the option meets any additional needs and whether the child is happy there.
Investigating the options in your area: research each option's type, cost, hours, registration and activities, then compare them in a table.
notes.tip: When asked to name and evaluate one option for working parents, work through these criteria in turn: cost, hours, location, safety, qualifications, reliability, activities and suitability. Finish by saying which family it suits.

notes.h: Evaluating two child care options (Higher Level only)
notes.b: An evaluation compares each option with the family's requirements, then weighs its advantages against its disadvantages. Any two options can be chosen, but a crèche and a childminder is the usual pair.
points: Step 1: identify the two options and the family requirements they must meet, such as hours, cost, reliability and the child's age.
Step 2: test each option against each requirement, rating how well it meets it.
Step 3: compare the options point by point; a crèche offers fixed hours and cover for absent staff, while a childminder offers flexibility and a home setting.
Step 4: identify which requirement decides the choice; for a family whose hours change often, flexibility may outweigh a crèche's structure.
Step 5: state the conclusion, showing which option suits which family and what the family must check before choosing.
Other pairs work too. An au pair is low cost and flexible in the home but untrained and short-term, while an after-school group is structured and registered but only covers after school.
A playschool, Montessori school or naíonra is educational and sociable, but runs only a few hours each day, so another arrangement is needed to cover the working day.
notes.tip: Higher Level questions want a balanced pair of advantages and disadvantages for each option, compared by the same criteria, with one overall conclusion. Do not just list options without evaluating them.

keyTerms.definition: The supervision, care and development of children while parents are at work or otherwise unable to care for them.
A centre-based day service that cares for children in groups during the working day.
An adult who cares for one or a small number of children in the minder's own home.
A young person, often from abroad, who lives with a family, provides childcare and does light household duties.
A service that collects children from school and cares for them until a parent is free to collect them.
A sessional pre-school service for young children, usually running for a few hours a day.
A pre-school approach that encourages children to learn through self-directed activity with structured materials.
An Irish-medium pre-school in which children learn through the Irish language.
How close a child care service is to the home or the workplace, which affects travel time.
The ability of a child care service to stay open and provide care when staff are ill or on leave.

factCards.term: Five factors that determine a family's child care requirements
factCards.definition: 1. Whether both parents or a lone parent are working. 2. Whether relatives are available to help. 3. Cost. 4. Hours needed, including after-school and holiday cover. 5. The child's age or special needs.

factCards.term: Four advantages of a crèche for a working family
factCards.definition: 1. Fixed daily opening hours. 2. Cover from several staff when one is absent. 3. Structured activities and peer play. 4. Staff with early-childhood qualifications.

1. The service depends on one adult, so illness or holidays leave no cover. 2. Planned educational activities may be narrower than in a larger centre. 3. The family must check the minder's training, safety and insurance.

factCards.term: Four criteria for evaluating any child care option
factCards.definition: 1. Cost and hours. 2. Hygiene and safety. 3. Staffing cover and reliability. 4. Staff qualifications and activities for the child's age.

factCards.term: Benefits of pre-school education for children
factCards.definition: Children become more socially aware, form relationships outside the home, grow more independent and confident, and develop intellectually and physically through play.

questions.prompt: Name two child care options available to working parents and state one advantage of each.
questions.model: Option 1 named, for example a crèche, with one advantage such as fixed daily opening hours or cover from several staff when one is absent. Option 2 named, for example a childminder, with one advantage such as a home setting, a small group or flexible hours. Two options and two advantages are needed for full marks.

questions.prompt: Evaluate two child care options available to a family in which both parents work full-time. Refer to cost, hours, reliability and the child's needs, and state which option you would recommend.
questions.model: Two options identified, for example a crèche and a childminder. Cost: the cost of each option, including fees and extras, weighed against the family's budget. Hours: a crèche's fixed hours against a childminder's possible flexibility for changing shifts. Reliability: a crèche's several staff giving cover for absence against a childminder depending on one adult. Child's needs: the benefit of group play and structured activities for a child's social and intellectual development, against the home setting and individual attention of a childminder. Recommendation: the option that best meets the family's stated requirements, with the reason given and the checks the family should make, such as staff qualifications, safety and cover arrangements.
